02Key achievements

What we have achieved

₹19 crore

Crossing 20,000 laptops

21,217 laptops received and 4,24,340 people reached across 22 states and 68 districts, over 40% of the way to 1 million. Refurbished laptops have saved NGOs and beneficiaries an estimated ₹19 crore against market prices.

₹10,000

The Saathi model is working

Shrutika now earns about ₹10,000 a month from her centre and Janki earned ₹7,000 in her first month. Self-help group leaders are asking us for laptops, and new centres are in the pipeline in Assam, Madhya Pradesh, Telangana and Chhattisgarh.

20

Renew Desk at Microsoft

On 29 October, 20 laptops were donated at Microsoft's Ferns office in Bengaluru for students through the Sama Laptop Grant, and employees signed up as mentors for the grant's pilot.

05In the pipeline

Coming next

Pilot under way

Sama Laptop Grant

An open call for young people doing meaningful work who need a laptop to do more of it. Each grantee receives a refurbished laptop and structured mentorship from employee volunteers. The pilot starts with Microsoft.

In design

Founders' first-laptop campaign

Startup founders share the story of their first laptop and fund one for the next builder: a freelancer, a creator or an early-stage founder. It runs on the same framework as the Laptop Grant.

07Perspective

India's laptop gap and its laptop surplus are the same conversation

< 1 in 10Indian households own a laptop or computer.
70 lakhcorporate laptops reach end of life in India every year.

A phone gets someone online. A laptop lets them write, code, apply and earn. Yet roughly 2 in 3 Indian women cannot send or receive an email, and most homes have never had a computer in them.

The devices exist. Computing equipment makes up nearly 70% of India's 1.41 million tonnes of annual e-waste, and much of it still has years of working life. Keeping a laptop in use for another 3 to 4 years avoids about 94% of the emissions of making a new one.

Reuse at scale needs three things: data-wiping standards that donors can trust, CSR and e-waste rules that put reuse ahead of recycling, and local partners who can put each device to work.

08Key learnings

What we have learned

  • 01

    From one-time drives to annual cycles

    Most of our corporate partnerships still begin and end with a single collection drive. Each drive matters, but impact grows fastest when laptop retirement becomes a planned part of a company's year.

    When a partner builds Sama into its annual IT refresh, we can plan refurbishment capacity ahead, commit devices to NGO partners with confidence, and show the company a fuller picture of what its laptops achieved over time.

  • 02

    Skills need devices

    India is betting big on digital and AI skills. On 15 August 2026 the Prime Minister announced that one crore youth would be trained in AI skills over the next year, and according to QS, the free YUVA AI for ALL programme under the IndiaAI Mission had drawn 8.5 million enrolments by July 2026.

    The device those skills depend on gets far less attention. Only 9.9% of Indian households own a computer, falling to 4.2% in rural areas, even though 95.1% own a mobile phone (CAMS 2022-23). Almost two-thirds of Indian women cannot send or receive an email (Comprehensive Modular Survey: Telecom 2025).

    This gap is why Sama exists. If computer access becomes part of national skilling policy, reusing corporate devices becomes part of the solution, and partners who donate laptops become part of India's AI skilling story.

  • 03

    Unlocking laptops in Special Economic Zones

    Many companies hold retired laptops inside SEZs, where moving them out for social use takes extra regulatory and financial steps and longer approvals. Working closely with corporates, we have found a way to bring these laptops out. A clearer policy route for social-purpose transfers would speed this up and open a large new source of devices for education.

  • 04

    Keeping technology affordable

    NGO partners pay only for refurbishment and logistics, not for the device. The cost of RAM and SSDs, the components we rely on most, has nearly tripled. We are working every day to keep laptops affordable so NGOs can spend their resources on their programmes, not on device procurement.

  • 05

    Building two-way NGO partnerships

    With 89 NGO partners, our relationships can centre on the moment a laptop is handed over. We want to be a long-term partner instead: staying close to how devices are used, learning from our partners' expertise on the ground, and collaborating beyond the first deployment. This also gives us richer impact data to share with you.

  • 06

    Learning to hire senior talent

    Senior hires are teaching us a lot, and we are still finding our way.

How partners can help

Commit devices on a predictable refresh schedule, bring employees in as mentors and volunteers, and introduce us to peers whose laptop fleets are due for renewal.
